teaser: She painted herself pregnant. She was not. And she signed without her husband's name.
review_notes:
Dated 25 May 1906, Paris; inscription 'Dies malte ich mit 30 Jahren an meinem 6. Hochzeitstage. P.B.'
Often called the first nude self-portrait by a woman painter in Western art: widely repeated, stated here as 'is thought to be'.
She is said to have sold only about three paintings in her lifetime, out of some 750: commonly cited figures.
Support: tempera on cardboard, about 101.8 x 70.2 cm.
Died 20 November 1907 of an embolism, 18 days after giving birth; last words 'Wie schade' are the traditional account.
Paula Modersohn-Becker Museum, Bremen, opened 1927, described as the first museum devoted to a woman painter.
Rilke, Requiem for a Friend, written 1908.

lesson.text: Thirty, six, zero. Thirty is her age, and six the years she has been married: she wrote both on the painting herself. Zero is the number of months she is pregnant. Paula Modersohn-Becker stands with her hands around a rounded belly, and there is no child in it.

The date is May 25, 1906. Three months earlier she had left her husband, the landscape painter Otto Modersohn, and their home in the artists' village of Worpswede in northern Germany. She took a train to Paris, rented a small studio, and wrote to a friend that she was no longer Modersohn and not yet anyone else.
She tells you all this in the picture, quietly, in one corner. The writing is faint and brown on the speckled wall, and most visitors walk past without noticing it.
She left a handwritten message on the painting. Can you spot it?

spots.title: Two lines and two letters
spots.text: In German: “I painted this at the age of 30 on my 6th wedding day. P.B.” Not P.M.B. On her wedding anniversary she signs with her maiden initials, Paula Becker, leaving Modersohn out.

lesson.text: So the anniversary portrait is a declaration of independence. And the belly? Most historians read it as an image of what she hoped to give birth to that year in Paris: herself as a painter. She wanted a child too, and said so in her letters. The painting holds both wishes without choosing.

There is another first here. A woman painting her own naked body, life-size, was almost unheard of in 1906. This is thought to be the first nude self-portrait by a woman in Western painting. For centuries women had been barred from life drawing classes, and the female nude was a subject painted by men for men.

In Paris she drew from nude models at private academies and at the anatomy classes of the École des Beaux-Arts, which had only opened its doors to women students a few years before. In Germany, most state academies still refused them.
The way she paints herself is as bold as the decision to do it. There is nothing seductive in the pose, and nothing apologetic either. Watch what she does with the body.

lesson.title: A body, not a pin-up
lesson.text: Three places where she refuses the usual rules of the nude.

spots.title: The belly
spots.text: A broad, golden oval with a tiny navel, pushed forward by her stance. It is painted in dry, grainy strokes, with no smooth blending to flatter it.

spots.title: The upper hand
spots.text: Her right hand rests above the belly, fingers curled. The knuckles are reddish and thick. These are working hands, painted with blunt honesty.

spots.title: The lower hand
spots.text: The other hand cups the belly from below, holding the white cloth at her hip. Together the two hands frame the oval the way you would hold something precious.

lesson.text: Those two hands turn the belly into the true subject of the picture. Everything else is kept simple so that it stays that way: a flat wall, a plain white cloth, a face with large dark eyes and almost no shading.

That simplicity was learned. In the Louvre she had studied Egyptian mummy portraits, painted nearly two thousand years earlier, with their wide eyes and calm frontal stare. In the galleries of Paris she discovered Cézanne and Gauguin, who built figures from solid blocks of color. She wanted, as she put it, great simplicity of form.

The surface looks chalky because it is not classic oil on canvas. She worked in tempera, a fast-drying paint bound with a water-based medium, on a sheet of cardboard about one meter (40 in) tall. The matte finish is close to a wall painting.
Now wander through the picture on your own. She kept the props to a minimum, so the few small things she did include carry meaning too: a necklace, a cloth, a patterned wall.

spots.title: The look
spots.text: Head tilted, eyes turned straight to you, a closed half-smile. She is not posing for a viewer. She is checking herself in a mirror, and seems rather pleased.

spots.title: Amber beads
spots.text: A long necklace of orange amber is the only thing she wears above the waist, and the strongest color in the painting. Its loop points down toward the belly.

spots.title: The white cloth
spots.text: Rough strokes of white and gray, tied low on the hips. It works like the drapery on an ancient statue and lifts the body up like a base.

spots.title: The speckled wall
spots.text: Green and yellow dabs on a pale ground, like wallpaper or spring leaves. The flat pattern keeps her body close to the surface, with no deep room behind.

spots.title: Hair, cut by the edge
spots.text: Her dark hair is parted, pinned up, and trimmed by the top of the board. The tight framing makes her fill the picture like a monument.

lesson.text: The freedom of that spring did not last. Otto followed her to Paris, and by 1907 she had returned to Worpswede with him. This time she was truly pregnant. Her daughter Mathilde was born on November 2, 1907.
Eighteen days later, allowed out of bed for the first time, Paula collapsed and died of an embolism, a blood clot. She was 31. Her last words are said to have been “Wie schade”: what a pity.

She is believed to have sold only about three paintings in her life, out of roughly 750 she made. Twenty years after her death, in 1927, a museum bearing her name opened in Bremen. It is considered the first museum in the world devoted to a woman painter.
A self-portrait can show a wish instead of a fact. She painted the person she intended to become, and signed it with the name she intended to keep.

Her friend, the poet Rainer Maria Rilke, wrote a long poem for her a year after she died, a requiem. In it he remembers how she undressed before the mirror and stepped into it, until only her looking was left. That is a fair description of what still stands in front of you.

quiz.question: Was Paula Modersohn-Becker pregnant when she painted this?
quiz.explanation: She painted an imagined pregnancy in May 1906; her daughter was born in November 1907.

quiz.question: What is unusual about the initials she signed?
options: She used her maiden initials, P.B.
quiz.explanation: On her wedding anniversary she left out the name Modersohn.

quiz.question: Which ancient works did she study in the Louvre?
quiz.explanation: Their wide eyes and calm stare shaped the way she painted faces.

quiz.question: What is the painting made with?
quiz.explanation: The fast-drying tempera gives the chalky, matte surface.

quiz.question: What is special about the museum in Bremen that bears her name?
options: It is the largest museum in Germany
It is considered the first museum devoted to a woman painter
It was built by her husband
quiz.explanation: It opened in 1927, twenty years after her death.

quiz.question: What is the strongest color accent on her body?
quiz.explanation: The orange amber beads are the only thing she wears above the waist.

facts.text: She painted this picture in Paris after leaving her husband.
facts.explanation: She had left Worpswede and Otto Modersohn three months earlier.

facts.text: She sold hundreds of paintings during her lifetime.
facts.explanation: She is believed to have sold only about three.

facts.text: The message on the painting gives her age as 30.
facts.explanation: She wrote that she painted it at 30, on her sixth wedding day.
